title: Half-Life and Nuclear Equations
description: Balance alpha and beta decay nuclear equations, and calculate remaining activity after a given number of half-lives.
hero_image_caption: Every unstable nucleus ticks down to its own rhythm — half-life governs everything from cancer treatment to the dating of ancient rocks.
content_html:
Isotopes and Unstable Nuclei

Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but they can have different numbers of neutrons. Atoms that differ only in neutron number are called isotopes. We represent a nucleus using standard notation: \(^{A}_{Z}X\), where \(A\) is the mass number and \(Z\) is the atomic number (proton number). For example, carbon-14 is written \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\): it has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Some isotopes are unstable — their nuclei have an unfavourable ratio of protons to neutrons and will spontaneously emit radiation to reach a more stable configuration. This process is called radioactive decay and is entirely random — it is impossible to predict exactly when any individual nucleus will decay.

Key Fact

In \(^A_Z X\) notation: A = mass number (protons + neutrons), Z = atomic number (protons only). The number of neutrons = A − Z. Memorise this — it is essential for balancing all nuclear equations.

Alpha Decay

In alpha decay, the nucleus emits an alpha particle, which is equivalent to a helium-4 nucleus (\(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\)). The parent nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2. The general form is: $$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$ Alpha particles are relatively massive and strongly ionising but have very low penetrating power — they are stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper.

Question: Radium-226 undergoes alpha decay. Write a balanced nuclear equation for this process. Radium has atomic number 88.

Step 1: Write the parent nucleus: \(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra}\).

Step 2: An alpha particle \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\) is emitted. Subtract from the parent:

  • Mass number of daughter = 226 − 4 = 222
  • Atomic number of daughter = 88 − 2 = 86

Step 3: Look up element 86: it is radon (Rn). Write the full equation: $$^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Check: Mass numbers: 226 = 222 + 4 ✓. Atomic numbers: 88 = 86 + 2 ✓. Both sides balance.

Beta Decay

In beta decay, a neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton, and a beta particle (high-speed electron, \(^{0}_{-1}\text{e}\)) is emitted. Because a neutron becomes a proton, the mass number stays the same but the atomic number increases by 1: $$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$ Beta particles are more penetrating than alpha particles — they are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium — but they are less ionising. Gamma radiation often accompanies both alpha and beta decay. Gamma rays (\(^{0}_{0}\gamma\)) carry no charge and have no mass, so they do not change the mass number or atomic number of the nucleus.

Question: Carbon-14 undergoes beta decay. Write a balanced nuclear equation. Carbon has atomic number 6.

Step 1: Write the parent: \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\).

Step 2: A beta particle \(^{0}_{-1}\text{e}\) is emitted. Add to atomic number:

  • Mass number of daughter = 14 + 0 = 14
  • Atomic number of daughter = 6 + 1 = 7

Step 3: Element 7 is nitrogen (N): $$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Check: Mass numbers: 14 = 14 + 0 ✓. Atomic numbers: 6 = 7 + (−1) ✓. This decay is used in radiocarbon dating of organic materials.

Half-Life

Because radioactive decay is random, we cannot predict when a single nucleus will decay. However, for a large sample, the half-life is the time for the activity — or the number of undecayed nuclei — to fall to half its initial value. Half-life is constant for a given isotope and does not depend on temperature, chemical state, or the size of the sample.

To calculate remaining activity or mass after \(n\) half-lives, use repeated halving: $$\text{remaining fraction} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$ For example, after 3 half-lives: \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}\) of the original activity remains. Alternatively, read from a half-life decay graph: the activity halves for each equal time interval equal to the half-life.

Key Fact

After \(n\) half-lives, the fraction of the original activity that remains is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\). After 1 half-life: ½. After 2: ¼. After 3: ⅛. After 4: 1/16. After 5: 1/32.

Half-Life Calculations

Half-life problems can ask you to: (a) find the remaining activity after a given number of half-lives, (b) find the number of half-lives that have passed, or (c) determine the half-life from a graph. For graph questions, identify any two points where the activity has halved and measure the time difference — this is one half-life. The graph of activity against time follows a characteristic curved shape called an exponential decay curve.

Half-life values range enormously across isotopes. Some isotopes have half-lives of fractions of a second; others persist for millions of years. This variation has practical consequences. Short half-lives are useful in medical imaging because the radioactivity clears the body quickly, minimising radiation dose to the patient. Long half-lives are useful in geological dating — the slow, predictable decay of long-lived isotopes like uranium-238 allows scientists to determine the age of ancient rocks with great precision. The key principle is that in each full half-life interval, exactly half the remaining undecayed nuclei will decay — no more, no less.
exam_tip_html: For nuclear equation questions, the most common error is not balancing both mass numbers AND atomic numbers. Check both sides separately: the sum of mass numbers on the left must equal the sum on the right, and the same for atomic numbers. For half-life calculations, write out the repeated halving step by step — do not try to shortcut. If a question gives you elapsed time and half-life, divide to find the number of half-lives, then apply (½)ⁿ. If asked to 'use the graph', read off values carefully and show the two points you used to determine the half-life.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alpha decay: mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2. Beta decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number increases by 1. Gamma emission changes neither.
  • Nuclear equations must balance on both sides: sum of mass numbers equal, and sum of atomic numbers equal.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. After n half-lives, remaining fraction = (½)ⁿ. Half-life is constant for a given isotope regardless of physical or chemical conditions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes an alpha particle?
A) A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus
B) A helium-4 nucleus containing 2 protons and 2 neutrons
C) A high-energy photon emitted from the nucleus
D) A single proton ejected from the nucleus
practice_questions.marks: B) A helium-4 nucleus containing 2 protons and 2 neutrons [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
practice_questions.marks: The time taken for the activity (or the number of undecayed nuclei) of a radioactive sample to decrease to half its original value. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the changes in mass number and atomic number that occur during beta decay.
practice_questions.marks: The mass number remains unchanged / does not change (1). The atomic number increases by 1 (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is not possible to predict exactly when a single radioactive nucleus will decay, yet the half-life of an isotope is a fixed and reliable value.
practice_questions.marks: Radioactive decay is a random process (1). It is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay (1). However, for a very large number of nuclei, the statistical average means that the time for exactly half of them to decay is consistent and constant — this is the half-life (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample has an initial activity of 640 Bq.
(a) Calculate the activity after 32 days.
(b) The same sample is used as a medical tracer. State one reason why a relatively short half-life is desirable for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Number of half-lives = 32 ÷ 8 = 4 (1). Remaining fraction = (½)⁴ = 1/16 (1). Activity = 640 ÷ 16 = 40 Bq (1). [3 marks]
(b) A short half-life means the radioactive material decays quickly so the patient is not exposed to radiation for a prolonged period / dose is minimised. [1 mark] [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Radium-226 undergoes alpha decay to produce radon. Radon then undergoes beta decay.
(a) Write a balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of radium-226. (Atomic number of Ra = 88.)
(b) Write a balanced nuclear equation for the subsequent beta decay of the radon isotope produced in part (a). (Atomic number of Rn = 86.)
(c) Explain the difference between contamination and irradiation as hazards associated with radioactive materials.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He [both numbers correct for 2 marks; 1 mark if one number is correct]
(b) ²²²₈₆Rn → ²²²₈₇Fr + ⁰₋₁e [both numbers correct for 2 marks; 1 mark if one number is correct — note: atomic number of daughter = 86 + 1 = 87, francium]
(c) Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; stops when source is removed. Contamination: radioactive material is deposited on or inside the body; continues to irradiate from within and is difficult to remove. Contamination is generally more hazardous because the source cannot be simply moved away. [2 marks — 1 for each correct distinction] [6 marks total]

knowledge_checks.q: Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay. By how much does its atomic number change?
A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 800 Bq. After 3 half-lives, what is its activity?
In beta decay, what happens to a neutron in the nucleus: _____
options: It is ejected directly from the nucleus
It splits into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted
It absorbs a proton to form a heavier neutron
It converts to a gamma ray
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is It splits into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted.

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement about half-life is correct: _____
options: Half-life increases as the sample cools down
Half-life depends on the chemical compound the element is in
Half-life is constant for a given isotope regardless of conditions
Half-life decreases as the sample gets older
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Half-life is constant for a given isotope regardless of conditions.

In beta decay, what happens to a neutron in the...
right: It splits into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

flashcard_questions.q: What changes in mass number and atomic number occur in alpha decay?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2. The nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons as a helium-4 nucleus.

flashcard_questions.q: What changes in mass number and atomic number occur in beta decay?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass number is unchanged; atomic number increases by 1. A neutron converts to a proton and an electron (beta particle) is emitted.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
flashcard_questions.a: The time taken for the activity of a radioactive sample to fall to half its initial value.

flashcard_questions.q: After 4 half-lives, what fraction of the original activity remains?
flashcard_questions.a: One sixteenth (1/16), found by halving four times: ½ → ¼ → ⅛ → 1/16.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is radioactive decay described as 'random'?
flashcard_questions.a: It is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay; each nucleus decays independently and spontaneously.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
flashcard_questions.a: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source and stops when the source is removed.

glossary_terms.definition: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus (nucleon number).
The number of protons in a nucleus, which determines the element.
The spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus.
A type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle (²₄He), losing 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
A type of radioactive decay in which a neutron converts to a proton and emits a fast-moving electron (beta particle).
The time taken for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) of a radioactive sample to decrease to half its initial value.
The number of nuclei that decay per second in a radioactive sample, measured in becquerels (Bq).
A curve showing activity decreasing by half for each successive half-life period.
